title: Extension points and maintainable code
idea: An extensible design adds features by plugging in new classes at a planned extension point; a maintainable one keeps each change small, local and easy to read.
points: Extension points are small interfaces where new classes plug in, often via a registry.
New behaviour arrives as a new class, registered at startup, with no core edits.
Maintainability comes from small classes, clear names and one place per decision.
Add an extension point only where change has already happened or is promised.

hero.title: Adding a format without touching the core

steps.caption: At startup, wiring code registers each exporter under a format name.
A caller asks the registry for a format. It never names a concrete class.
The registry looks up the format and calls `render(rows)` on the match.
Every exporter shares one method, `render`. That shared shape is the extension point.
A new format is one new class plus one `register` line. The registry and callers stay unchanged.

code.title: A registry of exporters
code.caption: Add a `TsvExporter` that joins values with `'\t'`, register it as `'tsv'`, and export again.

walk.text: The registry owns one decision: which exporter handles which format.
Duplicate names fail loudly instead of silently replacing an exporter.
No `switch` on format. Lookup replaces the branch that would grow forever.
Each exporter is a small class with one method, `render`.
Wiring lives in one place. A new format adds one class and one line here.
An unknown format fails with a clear message.

pitfalls: Do not add plugin hooks for changes nobody has asked for; it is speculative complexity.
A growing `switch` on a type string is the signal to introduce a registry.
Keep the extension interface small; every extra method burdens each new implementation.

quiz.why: A `Map` keeps one entry per key. The second `set('a')` replaces the first, which is why the registry guards against duplicates.

takeaway: Plan one small extension point; let new features arrive as new classes.
